product_line: UPMEM PIM DRAM modules with in-memory DRAM Processing Units (DPUs)

status.detail: A paper dated 2025-10-03 states that UPMEM was recently acquired by Qualcomm; a company database (rejected as evidence, kept as the only dated account) gives 2025-06-11. No announcement by Qualcomm or UPMEM was found, and the company website did not resolve from this session on 2026-10-09. What Qualcomm did with the product line is not known.

bets.text: Put general-purpose, C-programmable cores rather than fixed arithmetic units into a standard DRAM process and sell them on ordinary DDR4 modules, so servers, protocols and tools stay unchanged.
Cores without hardware floating point or wide multiply and divide are enough for the data-intensive workloads that matter.
The units need no direct interconnect; the host can carry all communication between them.
Volume production would bring the module premium over plain DRAM down from about tenfold to about one half.

generations.what_changed_from_previous: New chip interface, lower-power processor pipeline, repair and protection functions, the ability to boot as standard memory, and a scheme that makes the in-memory processors secure enclaves; the report says the specification was informed by use cases developed with commercial and research labs (u_cordis_2024).

sources.author: UPMEM (press release via Newswire)
sources.title_original: UPMEM Announces the First Processing In-Memory Chip Accelerating Big Data Applications
sources.summary_en: Founding announcement. A fabless Grenoble start-up describes a DRAM chip that carries its own small RISC processors (DRAM Processing Units) next to the memory array; the server CPU orchestrates many of them as co-processors and a software kit lets programmers dispatch tasks in high-level languages without changing hardware, protocols or tool flow. Targets data-intensive datacentre work, with genomics as the example. Gives an unconditioned speed-up claim and announces a Series A of about 3 million euros led by C4 Ventures with Partech, Supernova Invest, Western Digital Capital and Credit Agricole. No process, module format or dates.

sources.author: Timothy Prickett Morgan (The Next Platform)
sources.title_original: Putting In-Memory Processing Through The Paces
sources.summary_en: Article on the first application results UPMEM shared after Hot Chips 31. Describes the 8 GB DDR4 module (16 chips, 128 processing units, 64 MB of DRAM each), the core (14-stage pipeline, 24 hardware threads, no caches, small SRAM instruction and working memories, DMA between DRAM and core), and two customer workloads on a two-socket Xeon server with 128 GB of PIM: a search index sharded over 2,048 units and a genomics pipeline. Reports sampling in 2019 and mass production expected for mid-2020. The author adds what the vendor leaves out: a roughly tenfold module price premium, an unexplained offload method, a presumed accuracy trade in the tuned CPU baseline and untested server-level economics. Links only its own earlier article.

sources.author: Juan Gómez-Luna, Izzat El Hajj, Ivan Fernandez, Christina Giannoula, Geraldo F. Oliveira, Onur Mutlu
sources.title_original: Benchmarking a New Paradigm: An Experimental Analysis of a Real Processing-in-Memory Architecture
sources.summary_en: Independent characterisation of two real UPMEM servers (2,556 usable units at 350 MHz and 640 units at 267 MHz) with microbenchmarks and a 16-workload suite (PrIM); the abstract and the first 100,000 characters of the ar5iv HTML were read. Describes eight processing units per chip, each an in-order 32-bit RISC core with 24 hardware threads, a 64 MB DRAM bank, 24 KB instruction memory and 64 KB scratchpad, no caches, no hardware floating point or 32/64-bit multiply and divide, and no direct link between units (everything goes through the host over the memory bus). Concludes the design is compute-bound for anything heavier than integer addition, suits streaming, independently partitioned integer workloads, and scales poorly when units must communicate.

sources.author: Juan Gómez-Luna, Izzat El Hajj, Ivan Fernandez, Christina Giannoula, Geraldo F. Oliveira, Onur Mutlu
sources.title_original: Benchmarking Memory-Centric Computing Systems: Analysis of Real Processing-in-Memory Hardware
sources.summary_en: Invited workshop summary (CUT 2021) of the same study as u_prim_2021; only the abstract page was read and it carries no figures of its own. arXiv itself flags substantial text overlap with the longer paper, so it is listed as a duplicate and not counted as separate evidence.

sources.author: SAS UPMEM (periodic report summary published by the European Commission, CORDIS)
sources.date: reporting period 2022-12-01 to 2024-02-29 (the page shows a last-update date of 2023-03-03, which precedes the end of the period it reports on)
sources.title_original: ENERGIA/PIM: Accelerating Datacentre performance through Memory Chips to efficiently manage the Big Data Age - Periodic Reporting for period 2
sources.summary_en: Summary of the EIC-funded project (2022-03-01 to 2024-02-29, EU contribution about 2.5 million euros; page chrome in French, report text in English). UPMEM states that it finished the design of a new PIM chip and architecture: a new chip interface, a lower-power processor pipeline, repair and protection functions, the ability to boot as ordinary memory and a security scheme that turns the in-memory processors into enclaves, with control software and an updated module. Server integration was prepared with Intel, QCT and Supermicro; targets are big data and AI. Repeats vendor-level speed, efficiency and cost multiples without benchmark detail. No process node, tape-out or measured result.

sources.author: Krystian Chmielewski, Jarosław Ławnicki, Uladzislau Lukyanau, Tadeusz Kobus, Maciej Maciejewski (Huawei Technologies, Heterogeneous Memory Software Lab, Warsaw)
sources.title_original: UPMEM Unleashed: Software Secrets for Speed
sources.summary_en: arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed) by a Huawei lab measuring a 2,560-unit UPMEM-v1B server (2,551 working units, 400 MHz, up to 16 tasklets, SDK 2025.1.0). Shows that the vendor compiler leaves performance unused (hand-edited assembly speeds up integer add and multiply), that bit-serial INT4 arithmetic and NUMA-aware allocation help, and that quantised matrix-vector products beat a two-socket Arm server only when the matrix is already resident in PIM memory; with the transfer included the server wins. Confirms the absence of hardware 32-bit multiply/divide and floating point. States that UPMEM was recently acquired by Qualcomm.

sources.author: Niklas Klinger, Jonas Sander, Peterson Yuhala, Pascal Felber, Thomas Eisenbarth
sources.title_original: DRAMatic Speedup: Accelerating HE Operations on a Processing-in-Memory System
sources.summary_en: arXiv preprint (abstract only read) implementing the building blocks of homomorphic encryption on UPMEM hardware with residue-number and number-theoretic-transform techniques. Reports a large gain over earlier implementations on the same hardware and a comparison with Microsoft SEAL without figures. Names two hardware limits that still bind in 2026, host transfer overhead and slow multiplication, and discusses hardware extensions. Shows the hardware remained in research use after the acquisition.

sources.author: CB Insights
sources.summary_en: Company-database page listing Qualcomm as acquirer of UPMEM with the date 2025-06-11 and a history of funding rounds since 2017; amounts and investors are masked behind a subscription. No mechanism, no author and no primary link, so it is rejected as evidence and kept only as the single dated account of the acquisition.
